subject: anatomy
title: Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve, Parathyroid Glands, and Thoracic Duct

steps.tx: The recurrent laryngeal nerve exhibits marked anatomical asymmetry between the right and left sides of the body due to embryonic vascular remodelling. The right nerve loops around the right subclavian artery (remnant of the right fourth aortic arch), whereas the longer **left recurrent laryngeal nerve** loops beneath the arch of the aorta immediately behind the ligamentum arteriosum.
steps.say: Embryological remodelling creates asymmetry. The right nerve hooks around the subclavian artery, while the longer left nerve loops beneath the aortic arch behind the ligamentum arteriosum.

vis.alt: Anatomical schematic showing recurrent laryngeal nerve asymmetry, subclavian loop on right, and aortic arch loop on left
vis.caption: Bilateral trajectories of the recurrent laryngeal nerves and their relations to great vessels and thyroid lobes. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Both nerves ascend in or near the tracheo-oesophageal groove towards the lower pole of the thyroid lobes. In the neck, the **recurrent laryngeal nerve** is intimately related to the branches of the inferior thyroid artery, passing between, behind, or in front of them. The nerve enters the larynx deep to the lower border of the inferior constrictor muscle behind the cricothyroid joint.
steps.say: Ascending in the tracheoesophageal groove, each recurrent nerve intertwines with the inferior thyroid artery before entering the larynx behind the cricothyroid joint.

rows: Right subclavian artery (at root of neck)
Ascends through superior mediastinum behind pulmonary artery
Courses slightly more obliquely across groove
Runs strictly within the depth of the groove
Involved by apical lung or thyroid neoplasms
Involved by aortic aneurysms and left hilar bronchogenic carcinoma (Ortner syndrome)

steps.tx: Unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis fixes the ipsilateral vocal fold in the paramedian position, midway between abduction and adduction. The patient presents with hoarseness, a breathy voice, and a weakened cough. In contrast, bilateral **recurrent nerve** injury fixes both vocal cords in the paramedian position, precipitating acute inspiratory stridor that demands emergency tracheostomy.
steps.say: Unilateral recurrent nerve damage causes hoarseness with the cord in a paramedian stance. Bilateral paralysis causes emergency stridor and asphyxia requiring immediate tracheostomy.

left.title: Unilateral Recurrent Nerve Palsy
points: Ipsilateral vocal cord fixed in paramedian position
Contralateral cord compensates across midline over time
Voice: Hoarse, breathy, but airway remains adequate

right.title: Bilateral Recurrent Nerve Palsy
points: Both vocal cords fixed in paramedian position
Rima glottidis converted into narrow slit
Airway: Severe respiratory distress and inspiratory stridor
Demands immediate endotracheal intubation or tracheostomy

steps.tx: The parathyroid glands are four miniature endocrine bodies nestled on the posterior border of the thyroid lateral lobes, weighing thirty to forty milligrams each. The **superior parathyroid** glands (derived from the fourth pharyngeal pouch) occupy a constant position at the middle of the posterior border, lying dorsal to the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
steps.say: Four parathyroid glands rest along the posterior thyroid margin. The superior glands derive from the fourth pouch, occupying a constant dorsal position behind the recurrent nerve.

vis.alt: Anatomical schematic showing posterior surface of thyroid gland, parathyroid positions, and recurrent laryngeal nerve
vis.caption: Posterior aspect of the thyroid lobes displaying parathyroid glands and their arterial supply from the inferior thyroid artery. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The inferior parathyroid glands develop from the third pharyngeal pouch alongside the thymus, which migrates inferiorly into the anterior mediastinum. Consequently, the **inferior parathyroid** glands exhibit variable positions, typically resting near the inferior thyroid pole ventral to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, but occasionally descending with the thymus into the anterior mediastinum.
steps.say: Inferior parathyroid glands develop from the third pouch with the thymus. They lie ventral to the recurrent nerve but can migrate ectopically into the mediastinum.

rows: Constant: posterior border at level of cricoid cartilage
Lies DORSAL (posterior) to recurrent laryngeal nerve
Variable: lower pole of thyroid or thymic tongue
Lies VENTRAL (anterior) to recurrent laryngeal nerve
Terminal end branches form capsular rete

steps.tx: Accidental excision or devascularization of all four parathyroid glands during total thyroidectomy precipitates acute hypoparathyroidism. Within twenty-four to forty-eight hours, dropping serum ionic calcium levels trigger neuromuscular hyperexcitability, manifesting as perioral paresthesias, painful carpopedal spasms (Trousseau sign), and facial twitching upon tapping the facial nerve trunk (**Chvostek sign**).
steps.say: Postoperative hypoparathyroidism causes severe hypocalcaemia. Patients experience painful carpopedal spasms, perioral numbness, and positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs.

nodes.label: Iatrogenic Devascularization (Bilateral inferior thyroid artery ligation compromises parathyroid blood)
Hypocalcaemic Crisis (Serum ionic calcium drops below 7.0 mg/dL)
Neuromuscular Hyperexcitability (Low extracellular calcium increases neuronal membrane sodium permeability)
Tetany and Laryngospasm (Carpopedal spasm, Chvostek twitching, and life-threatening stridor)

steps.tx: At the root of the neck on the left side, the thoracic duct arches laterally from the superior mediastinum at the level of the transverse process of C7. Ascending behind the carotid sheath, the **thoracic duct** arches anterior to the vertebral artery, thyrocervical trunk, phrenic nerve, and scalenus anterior muscle, passing between the common carotid artery and left subclavian artery.
steps.say: At the root of the left neck, the thoracic duct arches forward behind the carotid sheath. It curves anterior to the vertebral vessels and phrenic nerve.

vis.alt: Anatomical schematic tracing the thoracic duct arching in the left root of the neck to enter venous confluence
vis.caption: Anatomical course and left cervical arch of the thoracic duct terminating at the internal jugular-subclavian junction. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The thoracic duct terminates by opening into the junction of the left internal jugular vein and left subclavian vein (the venous angle or angle of Pirogov). Guarded by a bicuspid valve that prevents reflux of venous blood into the lymphatic channel, the **thoracic duct arch** can be lacerated during radical left block neck dissections, resulting in a persistent, high-volume milky chylous fistula.
steps.say: The thoracic duct terminates at the left venous angle between the jugular and subclavian veins. Inadvertent surgical transection creates a high-volume chylous fistula.

nodes.label: Left Cervical Arch (Rises 3-4 cm above clavicle behind carotid sheath)
Anterior Crossing (Passes over phrenic nerve and scalenus anterior)
Venous Angle of Pirogov (Enters confluence of left IJV and subclavian vein)
Bicuspid Valve (Prevents retrograde entry of venous blood into lymphatic trunk)
